title: Vishnu Sahasranamam Lyrics with Meaning: Verses 89-90
desc: Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 89 to 90 in Sanskrit with a simple English meaning and how to chant them: 'सहस्रार्चिः सप्तजिह्वः सप्तैधाः सप्तवाहनः'.
alt: Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 89 to 90 with meaning
caption: Vishnu Sahasranamam, verses 89 to 90.
intro: **Vishnu Sahasranamam** is the thousand names of Lord Vishnu, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata. This post gives **verses 89 to 90** with the Sanskrit text and a plain English meaning, so you can chant with understanding.
takeaways: The verses here open with **सहस्रार्चिः सप्तजिह्वः सप्तैधाः सप्तवाहनः**.
Read the Sanskrit slowly, then the meaning, then chant once more.
Thursday and Ekadashi are the days most families keep for Vishnu Sahasranamam.
A short daily portion is better than a rushed full reading.

p: Read the lines aloud, one breath for each half of a verse:
**सहस्रार्चिः सप्तजिह्वः सप्तैधाः सप्तवाहनः । अमूर्तिरनघोऽचिन्त्यो भयकृद्भयनाशनः ॥** **अणुर्बृहत्कृशः स्थूलो गुणभृन्निर्गुणो महान् । अधृतः स्वधृतः स्वास्यः प्राग्वंशो वंशवर्धनः ॥**

He has a thousand rays, seven tongues, seven fuels and seven steeds. Formless, sinless and beyond thought is that God of gods. He is the cause of fear, and he is its destroyer. Smaller than an atom, vaster than the vast, slender and massive is he. He bears every quality yet has none, the great one, that God of gods. Held up by none, he upholds himself, fair of face, the ancient line and the one who makes it flourish.
Light a lamp, sit facing east and chant these verses once, then read the meaning silently. Many families take two verses a day and finish the full text in a little under two months.
The names do not need a long ritual. What matters is steady practice, a clear pronunciation and a calm mind.

ul: Thursdays, the day of Vishnu and the planet Jupiter.
Early morning after a bath, or in the evening at the lamp.

faq.q: What do Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 89 to 90 mean?
faq.a: He has a thousand rays, seven tongues, seven fuels and seven steeds. Formless, sinless and beyond thought is that God of gods. He is the cause of fear, and he is its destroyer. Smaller than an atom, vaster than the vast, slender and massive is he. He bears every quality yet has none, the great one, that God of gods. Held up by none, he upholds himself, fair of face, the ancient line and the one who makes it flourish.
**Bhishma** taught it to Yudhishthira on the field of Kurukshetra, as told in the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata.

faq.q: Can I chant a few verses a day instead of the whole text?
faq.a: Yes. A small daily portion with the meaning understood is a common and accepted way to learn it.

note: The Sanskrit is the traditional text. The English is our own plain rendering of the meaning.
